case_study_insert.main_stem: Eastmere Eco-Laminates (ELC) is a cooperative in the sustainable building materials sector, employing a workforce of 45. Founded in 2015 by Noor Eastmere, the business makes recycled-fibre insulation panels for house builders and operates a flat structure with laissez-faire leadership. ELC plans to invest $1,200,000 in a recycled-fibre panel plant using eco-packaging, financed by a $700,000 share issue and a $500,000 bank overdraft. It has fixed costs of $450,000 a year, a variable cost of $14.00 a unit and a selling price of $23.00, and currently produces 90,000 units a year. ELC faces a rising defect rate in panel bonding and complaints about delivery damage to panels arriving at busy building sites.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Quality Report — Q2 2025: The panel line produced 22,500 panels last quarter at a defect rate of 3.1%, down from 4.7% a year ago. Delivery-damage complaints fell from 28 to 11 per month. Average lead time is 6.2 days. A survey of 350 builders found that 71% would pay up to $1.50 more for recycled-fibre panels, and 57% check environmental claims before specifying materials. A skills audit shows 16 of 45 members have not been trained on the new bonding presses; college courses cost $1,250 per employee.

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.0% to 4.75%, raising the cost of overdraft borrowing. (2) The national minimum wage will increase by 6.9% from $13.10 to $14.00 per hour from April 2026, lifting wage costs. (3) Recycled-fibre and resin input costs have risen 10.3% year-on-year, while construction output grew 2.4% over the same period.

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages for ELC of funding the panel plant with a share issue rather than a bank overdraft.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A $700,000 share issue provides permanent capital with no interest or repayment schedule, protecting ELC's cash flow while it meets $450,000 of fixed costs a year. A $500,000 bank overdraft would charge interest at a rate linked to the 4.75% base rate and could be withdrawn on demand; share funds instead let the full $9.00 contribution on each panel stay in the cooperative to absorb the 10.3% rise in recycled-fibre and resin costs without increasing the $23.00 price to builders.

Point 2: Share capital does not require security over the cooperative's assets, so the $1,200,000 panel plant is safe from seizure if construction demand falls, which matters while the 3.1% bonding defect rate persists. An overdraft is a short-term source ill-suited to a long-lived plant and could leave ELC exposed if the bank cuts its facility. Equity from members also aligns ownership with the cooperative's sustainable aims, keeping control of the eco-packaging strategy inside the business rather than with an external lender.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation applied to the named business.

questions.question_text: Consider trade magazine advertising, sponsorship of building exhibitions, or social media campaigns. Which should ELC choose to promote its recycled-fibre panels? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Trade magazine advertising: Specialist building titles reach the 350 builders surveyed and other specifiers with a detailed technical message about recycled-fibre panels. Costs are moderate and the message endures, but print cannot demonstrate panel performance, has long lead times and may not shift the 90,000-unit target quickly in a market where 57% check environmental claims.

Sponsoring building exhibitions: Exhibitions let ELC show the panels, meet house builders face to face and explain the 71% willingness to pay $1.50 more, directly supporting specification decisions. Sponsorship and stand costs are high for a cooperative with a $500,000 overdraft, and benefits last only for the event, so the cost per sustained lead may be poor.

Social media campaigns: Targeted posts can present the recycled-fibre and eco-packaging story to sustainability-minded builders, with precise measurement and low cost per contact. Content can be updated fast and shared nationally, though builders may trust technical specifications and peer recommendations more than online ads, and online interest does not automatically become orders.

Recommendation: ELC should choose social media campaigns, reinforced by technical leaflets sent to specifiers. They reach the 71% of builders who value recycled-fibre panels at low cost and travel further than an exhibition stand. Exhibitions are rejected as costly and short-lived while an overdraft must be managed; trade magazines are rejected as slow and unable to demonstrate the $1.50 environmental premium, while leaflets supply the technical detail social media cannot hold. Protecting the $9.00 contribution matters while the $500,000 overdraft is outstanding and 90,000 panels must be sold each year.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies promotional options with limited application to ELC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discusses advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of ELC with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three options in the context of ELC with a well-justified recommendation explaining why exhibitions and print are rejected.

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits for ELC of using team working to cut its panel bonding defects and delivery-damage complaints.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Team working gives the 45 members joint responsibility for a finished panel, so bonding faults are caught by colleagues before dispatch. This can push the 3.1% defect rate lower and reduce the 11 monthly delivery-damage complaints, because teams check each other's work and packaging together. It fits the flat structure and laissez-faire leadership in the case, where members are expected to organise their own work.

Point 2: Teams provide social support and shared decision-making, which can raise motivation among members and reduce the disruption caused by the 16 who lack training on the bonding presses. Experienced members can coach others on the line, making the $1,250 college courses more targeted, while shared ownership of output protects the 22,500 panels made last quarter and the 90,000-unit annual target for Noor Eastmere's cooperative. This also underpins the $1,200,000 plant, while the flat structure lets teams act on their own ideas without waiting for approval.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation applied to the named business.

questions.question_text: Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the local college for the 16 members. Which should ELC choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Coaching at the bonding presses is specific to ELC's own plant, costs no fees and keeps the 16 members productive while learning, protecting the 22,500 panels made last quarter and the improvement to a 3.1% defect rate. Its weaknesses are that mentor-members lose production time, poor technique can be copied, and there is no formal certificate if builders ask for evidence of competence.

Off-the-job training: A local college course at $1,250 per employee gives structured skills and a recognised certificate for all 16 members, costing $20,000 in total — small against the $1,200,000 plant. However, it removes 16 of 45 members from production, cutting capacity when 90,000 panels are needed, and generic content may not match ELC's bonding presses, so on-site follow-up would still be needed.

Decision: ELC should choose on-the-job training initially, with short college modules for team coordinators later. It is cheaper, plant-specific and avoids losing output while defects and delivery damage are active concerns; full off-the-job training is rejected because releasing 16 members and spending $20,000 would disrupt supply to house builders, and certification can be added once the new plant is running smoothly.

Additional considerations: Because ELC is a cooperative with laissez-faire leadership, members may respond better to peer coaching on the bonding presses than to formal classroom instruction, strengthening the case for on-the-job learning. Yet builders increasingly demand evidence of competence, so the $1,250 college certificate has real commercial value. A blended route of college modules for coordinators then on-site coaching for all 16 members keeps the 90,000-panel target while meeting buyer expectations.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to ELC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both methods in the context of ELC.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods in the context of ELC with a justified decision covering cost, disruption and plant relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how ELC's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.
questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 50,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $9.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety against 90,000-unit output; pricing and discount modelling against $450,000 fixed costs; overdraft and share-finance feasibility for the $1,200,000 plant; and unit cost of $19.00 with productivity of 2,000 units per worker, used to tackle the 3.1% defect rate.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $450,000 ÷ ($23.00 − $14.00) = $450,000 ÷ $9.00 = 50,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 50,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $23.00 − $14.00 = $9.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $9.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways ELC's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 50,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 90,000 units, a margin of safety of 40,000 units, to justify the $1,200,000 panel plant.
2. Contribution of $9.00 lets managers test a builder discount: a $1.50 concession leaves $7.50 per panel, showing the extra volume needed to cover $450,000 fixed costs.
3. Fixed costs and contribution set the output needed to service the $500,000 overdraft and justify the $700,000 share issue.
4. Unit cost of $450,000 ÷ 90,000 + $14.00 = $19.00 and productivity of 90,000 ÷ 45 = 2,000 units per worker allow weekly benchmarking and help reduce the 3.1% bonding defect rate.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate ELC's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Which ratio provides the stronger evidence of improvement? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 30.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 33.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 15.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 18.0%
ROCE 2024 = 18.0%
ROCE 2025 = 21.6%

Detailed workings: In 2024 gross profit of $2,250,000 = revenue $7,500,000 − cost of sales $5,250,000; $2,250,000 ÷ $7,500,000 = 30.0%. In 2025 gross profit of $2,970,000 = revenue $9,000,000 − cost of sales $6,030,000; $2,970,000 ÷ $9,000,000 = 33.0%. Operating profit rose from $1,125,000 to $1,620,000; $1,125,000 ÷ $7,500,000 = 15.0% and $1,620,000 ÷ $9,000,000 = 18.0%. Capital employed moved from $6,250,000 to $7,500,000; $1,125,000 ÷ $6,250,000 = 18.0% and $1,620,000 ÷ $7,500,000 = 21.6%. Interest payable was $150,000 then $180,000.

Evaluation: All three measures improved, so ELC's profitability strengthened. Gross profitability rose from 30.0% to 33.0%, consistent with better control of fibre and resin costs as the 3.1% defect rate fell. The operating return on sales improved from 15.0% to 18.0%, showing the $450,000 fixed costs are absorbed by output of 90,000 panels. Return on capital rose from 18.0% to 21.6% despite capital employed reaching $7,500,000 to fund the $1,200,000 plant, so the eco-packaging investment is adding value.

Stronger evidence: the profit margin, because it gained three percentage points straight from the given revenue and operating profit and is less affected than returns measured against a capital base enlarged by the $700,000 share issue.

Conclusion: ELC's financial performance has improved across all three measures. The operating return on sales is the clearest indicator of efficiency; the caution is the $500,000 overdraft and rising interest payable, which must still be covered from the stronger margins.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the three ratios for both years with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years, detailed evaluation of revenue, cost and capital movements, and a justified conclusion naming the stronger evidence.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for ELC of using recycled-fibre materials and eco-packaging in its panels.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Recycled-fibre panels appeal to the 71% of 350 builders who would pay $1.50 more, allowing ELC to defend its $9.00 contribution per unit while fibre and resin input costs rise 10.3%. The 57% who check environmental claims make the eco-packaging a strong differentiator when competing for house-builder contracts, supporting the $23.00 price and the $1,200,000 plant.

Disadvantage: Recycled fibre and eco-packaging may cost more or vary in quality, which would raise the $14.00 variable cost per unit and squeeze margins unless the full $1.50 premium is won. Inconsistent material could worsen the 3.1% bonding defect rate or increase the 11 monthly delivery-damage complaints, adding cost while the $500,000 overdraft still needs servicing. The cooperative has already committed $700,000 of share capital to the $1,200,000 plant, so defending the $9.00 contribution is essential for servicing that overdraft, sustaining output of 90,000 panels and meeting the environmental expectations of its members.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation applied to the named business.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 4.75%, the 6.9% minimum wage increase and the 10.3% rise in recycled-fibre and resin input costs will affect ELC. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Base interest rate (4.0% to 4.75%): ELC's $500,000 bank overdraft is interest-bearing and linked to the base rate, so the 0.75 percentage point rise adds 0.0075 × $500,000 = $3,750 a year. That is modest against $450,000 of fixed costs, but unlike a fixed loan an overdraft rate can move quickly, so the cooperative should try to replace part of it with cheaper long-term finance.

Minimum wage (6.9%, to $14.00 from $13.10 per hour): With a workforce of 45, this feeds into wage bills and cannot be avoided. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay rates, so an annual total cannot be honestly computed; the defensible test is productivity of 90,000 units ÷ 45 members = 2,000 units per worker. If productivity holds, the rise is absorbable; if it slips, unit labour cost rises and the $9.00 contribution narrows.

Input cost inflation (10.3% recycled fibre and resin): The insert does not decompose the $14.00 variable cost, so only a bound can be calculated: if all of it rose 10.3%, that adds 10.3% × $14.00 = $1.44 per unit; across 90,000 panels that is about $129,600 a year (90,000 × $1.44). The $1.50 environmental premium can recover only part of this, while construction output grew just 2.4%.

Conclusion: The 10.3% input-cost rise has the greatest impact because it applies to every one of the 90,000 panels and directly attacks the $9.00 contribution funding the $1,200,000 plant. The overdraft interest effect is smaller and can be refinanced, and the wage rise can be offset if productivity holds, whereas input inflation hits unit economics with limited pricing power.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the three external changes with limited application to ELC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on ELC's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes in the context of ELC with a well-justified judgment that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact.
